findings.title: Options object flips rejectOnClear default to rejecting queued promises
findings.cause: The options destructuring now defaults rejectOnClear to true when an options object is used: `({concurrency, rejectOnClear = true} = concurrency);`.
findings.impact: Callers using the documented `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` form now get AbortError rejections from `clearQueue()` even though the README and type docs say rejectOnClear defaults to false. This is a visible API behavior regression and can break shutdown/teardown code that intentionally discards pending tasks without awaiting them.
findings.evidence: Current source index.js:6-8 sets the object-option default to true. README readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 document `Default: false`. Focused probe with `pLimit({concurrency:1})`, one running task, one pending task, then `clearQueue()` produced `AbortError` instead of leaving the pending promise unsettled.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit=pLimit({concurrency:1}); limit(()=>new Promise(()=>{})); const pending=limit(()=>Promise.resolve('pending')); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); console.log(await Promise.race([pending.then(()=> 'resolved', error => error?.name || 'rejected'), new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(()=>resolve('pending-after-clear'), 50))]));" # observed: AbortError; expected: pending-after-clear

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass runtime validation
findings.cause: Validation was changed to `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`, so only truthy invalid values are rejected.
findings.impact: Invalid API inputs such as `rejectOnClear: ''`, `0`, or `null` are accepted and silently treated as disabled. That weakens the documented boolean contract and makes configuration mistakes hard to detect.
findings.evidence: Current source index.js:12 only validates invalid truthy values. README readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 say the option type is boolean. The committed baseline validated `typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean'` unconditionally.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of ['', 0, null]) { try { pLimit({concurrency:1, rejectOnClear:value}); console.log(String(value)+':accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log(String(value)+':'+error.name); } }" # observed: all accepted; expected: TypeError for each non-boolean

findings.title: limit.map omits indexes for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call now passes `iterableIsArray ? index : undefined`, so Sets, array iterators, generators, and other iterables receive `undefined` instead of their iteration index.
findings.impact: The public contract says the mapper receives both item value and index for any iterable. Non-array iterable users get wrong results whenever they depend on the index, while the current tests only assert non-array values and miss index behavior.
findings.evidence: Current source index.js:107-112 conditionally drops the index. README readme.md:78-84 and index.d.ts:30-43 state that the mapper receives the item value and its index and describe equivalence to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => ...)`. Tests at test.js:239-255 cover Set/iterator values but do not assert the index.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit=pLimit(1); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(new Set(['a','b','c']), (_value,index)=>index))); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(['a','b','c'].values(), (_value,index)=>index)));" # observed: [null,null,null] because index is undefined; expected: [0,1,2]

findings.title: limitFunction drops all caller arguments
findings.cause: The returned wrapper was changed from forwarding `...arguments_` into the original function to `return () => limit(() => function_());`.
findings.impact: Any limited function that needs parameters now receives none. This breaks the documented generic TypeScript signature and the recipe pattern `urls.map(url => limitedFetchUrl(url))`, causing real workloads to fetch/process `undefined`.
findings.evidence: Current source index.js:121-124 returns a zero-argument wrapper. index.d.ts:133-136 declares the returned function as `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`. recipes.md:161-163 demonstrates passing a URL argument into the limited function.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited=limitFunction(async value => value, {concurrency:1}); console.log(await limited('sentinel'));" # observed: undefined; expected: sentinel

findings.title: Infinity concurrency is rejected despite prior unlimited-concurrency support
findings.cause: Validation now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency) && concurrency > 0`, removing the previous explicit `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` allowance.
findings.impact: Callers that use `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` to disable limiting or select an effectively unlimited limiter now get a synchronous TypeError. This is a backward-incompatible behavior regression relative to the committed implementation.
findings.evidence: Current source index.js:127-130 rejects all non-integers, including Infinity. The committed baseline from `git show HEAD:index.js` allowed `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0` at lines 123-125.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { const limit=pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY); console.log('accepted', typeof limit); } catch (error) { console.log('threw', error.message); }" # observed: threw Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up; expected: accepted function

Ranked index.js as the highest combined-risk module and exposed p-limit internal functions.
First batch used wrong parameter names; retried with live-schema names. Separate isolated probe runs start cold, so validate_plan without ingest reported blocked/needs recovery.

With ingest in the same run, glob found JS files, seek routed to validateConcurrency/enqueue/limitFunction, and impact showed index.js affects resumeNext, next, run, result, enqueue, generator, limitFunction, and validateConcurrency.

Called after a blocked literal search. Because the helper uses a new isolated runtime per command, the playbook correctly reported needs_ingest for that fresh process; final truth was verified by direct source reads and focused Node probes.

agent_testimony: I did not read operator-only artifacts and did not patch the audited repo. m1nd was useful for trust establishment, workspace binding checks, repo orientation, and identifying index.js as the critical surface. Its isolated probe helper starts a fresh runtime per command, so I ingested within multi-call runs and treated cold-runtime recovery output as a helper/runtime note rather than repo evidence. Final findings are based on direct source/contract reads, git diff against HEAD, and focused Node probes.
